articles.title: We’ll Miss You, Tim Curry! Remembering the Late Actor with His 5 Best Roles, Ranked
articles.content:
Tim Curry, the smooth-voiced English actor known for his big roles, bigger smile and thoughtful demeanor, has died at the age of 80.
Forever associated with The Rocky Horror Picture Show, Curry brought that all-in exuberance to every role he played—even if Curry himself was a bit more reserved. But the cheeky humor we loved in roles from Clue to Broadway’s Spamalot was there all along, even as he suffered health setbacks in the last decade or so of his life: “The day before I had the stroke, I smoked three packs of Marlboro Reds,” he told the Guardian just last year. “I won’t be doing that again!”
I’ve been a Tim Curry fan since I was in middle school (Clue, again), but it was the audience-participation recordings of Rocky Horror that sealed the deal. I discovered them when I was a high school exchange student half a world from home, and something about the inclusive party atmosphere, and Curry’s enigmatic, winking portrayal of Dr. Frank-N-Furter, kept me from feeling lonely. I listened to them so often that when I pulled them out this summer for a road trip, I still knew every word.
Curry was a huge part of those memories, and he somehow inhabited a timeless space in my mind, so the news of his death was a shock. He also showed up everywhere, playing villains (Charlie’s Angels) and bumbling British cretins (Home Alone 2) and doing so much voice work that it’s amazing he still had a voice left. It’s hard to pick his top five roles, but let’s try, shall we? Read on as we count down to our No. 1 pick.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity news, entertainment, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Curry is often celebrated for his comedy, but let’s start with a drama—he’s just that versatile. In this Ridley Scott dark fantasy film starring Tom Cruise, Curry gets to flex his villain chops as the Lord of Darkness, a cloven-hoofed demon who wants to, well, plunge the world into darkness.
Curry reportedly spent five-and-a-half hours in makeup every day getting transformed into the unicorn-hating antagonist. And even though the movie was a box-office disappointment, it surely wasn’t due to Curry’s performance, which audiences loved. The movie also went on to be nominated for multiple awards for makeup and music.
Any time you can get Tim Curry, Bernadette Peters and Carol Burnett in the same room together, you know they’re going to deliver a showstopper. And that’s just what they did in 1982’s Annie. Curry plays Rooster, the smarmy brother to Burnett’s Miss Hannigan, and he oozes sleaze from every pore as he and his dimwit girlfriend, Lily (Peters), scheme to kidnap little orphan Annie.
Curry is outstanding in this big-budget movie version of the Broadway megahit, which was based on the long-running comic strip set during the Depression. Even surrounded by Broadway titans like Ann Reinking and Albert Finney, Curry runs away with this film. And when the nefarious trio of kidnappers, led by Curry, belts out “Easy Street,” dreaming of the day they can cash in on the reward offered by Daddy Warbucks, you know you’re in the presence of greatness.
I will never forget seeing this one in the movie theater—perhaps because I went back the very next day to see it again—and I have since watched it dozens of times. Based on the popular board game of the same name, Curry plays Wadsworth, the butler at a stodgy English estate who must wrangle an unruly group of guests who are all suspected of murder.
Filled with memorable one-liners (“flames on the side of my face,” anyone?), Clue was released with three different endings, mirroring the board game’s possible outcomes, and mixed reviews. It has since become a major cult favorite, and Curry’s bemused, rat-a-tat-tat delivery is one reason why. When asked what a butler does, he quips, “I buttle.” After he launches into a long explanation of the crime, he says, “And to make a long story short …,” to which the entire cast retorts, “Too late.”
I can barely write about this one. Curry plays Pennywise, an ancient evil being that takes the form of a demented killer clown who lives in the sewers. The 1990 television miniseries was adapted from Stephen King’s novel, and more than 37 million people watched this primetime show, which was on regular television, not cable or streaming, for two whole frightening nights.
Curry was so good in the role that in his memoir, he said people often came up to him to tell him how traumatized they were, even decades later. “But I’ve never really known how to respond to that,” he wrote in his characteristically dry and thoughtful manner. “It’s not the most charming conversation starter, and invariably leads to a less-than-delightful discussion to navigate.”
Talk about a cult favorite! This low-budget monster-movie spoof stars Curry as Dr. Frank-N-Furter, a cross-dressing mad scientist whose home Brad and Janet (Barry Bostwick and Susan Sarandon) seek shelter in when their car breaks down. Things get absolutely wonderful from there, as the naive couple realizes they’ve stumbled into a party filled with characters not found at the junior chamber of commerce.
As the music (and antici … pation) builds, a caped Curry in full makeup drops into the scene in a caged elevator. Janet faints, and he introduces himself with a booming baritone: “How’d you do, I … see you’ve met my … faithful handy-man” and launches into “Sweet Transvestite,” a song about accepting people for who they are. It’s just one of Curry’s many iconic moments in this tiny movie (and before that, a London stage play) that became a sensation with audiences, if not critics.
The Rocky Horror Picture Show can still be seen in theaters more than 50 years after it was released, often around Halloween. Curry also lent his voice to a Fox television remake, and Dr. Frank-N-Furter has become so heavily associated with Curry that he was often asked about his legacy as the fishnet-wearing doc. In his characteristically understated way, he told the Los Angeles Times: “There’s not a lot I can do about it really.”
That’s how we feel about losing you, Mr. Curry.

白羊座：秋分时节，你的合作领域被激活，这意味着你渴望寻找伙伴。无论是想与朋友合作创业、与同事推进职业目标，还是将浪漫关系带到新阶段，现在都风驰电掣。尽管你擅长独自飞行，但在一对一的关系中展示自己可以帮助你在最雄心勃勃的目标上取得突破，这对你的野心至关重要。需要警惕的是，秋分后不久满月将落在你的自我宫位，情绪可能会高涨。你可能会倾向于通过运动或投入工作来应对挑战，但认真面对任何需要疗愈的情感痛苦才是最好的选择。可以联系心理治疗师进行压力管理，或将心中所想倾注于想象力的创作，如手工艺、绘画、舞蹈或写日记。

金牛座：作为金星的星座，你对亲友忠诚至深，且偏爱在家招待。但要做好准备：太阳进入同属金星星座的天秤座和日常生活宫位，秋分将让你奔波于一个又一个的约会、健身或社交活动。尽管这可能让你有点焦虑，因为你通常更喜欢在沙发上窝着而不是出门，但你以慢而稳的节奏处理事情的能力将确保你胜任。金星将在10月25日前继续影响你的合作领域，向伴侣、朋友或可信赖的同事求助将有助于减轻负担。无论是需要帮忙准备义卖还是陪伴晨间散步，你都会感到格外支持。

双子座：欢迎进入更多乐趣、创造力和玩乐的时刻，因为2026年的秋分星盘将提升你的快乐感！太阳将进入你的浪漫与自我表达宫位——一个轻松愉快的区域，将放大你的艺术冲动和更自发、轻松的特质（是的，真的）。这意味着你会渴望对朋友的临时Airbnb预订或与伴侣的浪漫周末旅行说"yes"。你的守护星水星也将在这里，将你的思维能量引向更多心领神会的方式。如果你能想到，就能实现。由于太阳与反叛的天王星在你的星座和谐相处，你将感受到走自己的路的力量。你可能会受到鼓舞，尝试换季服饰或投入到让你感到真正灵感涌动的艺术项目中。

巨蟹座：尽管你已经注重与亲友共度时光和享受家的舒适，但秋分将为你的家庭纽带带来更多和谐。太阳照亮你的家庭生活宫位，使得与亲人联系、培养安全感和照顾情感健康更加容易。平息与家人的任何持续冲突、为环境注入更多美感、沉浸在秋季传统中——如用菊花和南瓜装饰门廊或制作最爱的食谱——都显得直觉正确。你可能会更加中心和快乐，因为这种怀旧、舒适的氛围与你的天性相符。感受更多创造力和与亲友的自发性也在预期之中，多亏金星在10月25日前位于你的浪漫宫位。你还可以期待火星即将进入你的收入宫位，这将增强你争取更多收入机会的能力。

天蝎座：尽管你一年四季都重视隐私、亲密关系和内心梦想生活，但在秋分时节，你将比往常更加保守，因为太阳进入你的精神宫位。这一领域关注沉思和心理健康，因此考虑反思如何更好地照顾长期以来携带的情感创伤。虽然这听起来有些孤独，但金星将在10月25日前位于你的星座，你也能在需要时依靠亲友倾诉感受。你还会发现，为生活注入更多愉悦和舒适变得更加容易。需要注意的是：火星将在秋分后几天，即9月27日进入你的事业宫位，增强你追求宏图目标和赢得上级认可的能量。你可能会被赋能担任领导职位或重新定义成功的意义。

射手座：更欢乐、充满乐趣的与朋友共度时光总是你的目标，而2026年的秋分正好带给你这个机会，因为太阳进入你的友谊宫位，月亮激活你的沟通宫位。这是你每年将更多精力投入到纯真友谊的契机，做一个团队合作者，与社区建立联系，并在过程中拓展人脉。将你天生的全或不全的态度投入这些努力，也将为你实现长期愿望铺平道路——秋分星盘激活的另一个生活领域。你还可以利用火星，即将在9月27日进入你的冒险、哲学和高等教育宫位。接下来的两个月，你可以比平时更大胆地走出舒适区，吸收知识。考虑预订一次远程旅行、与激励人心的导师合作或追求更高学位。

摩羯座：作为勤奋的星座，这一年对你来说特别令人兴奋，因为太阳正穿过你的事业和公众形象宫位。无论你渴望上级认可你在工作中的努力，还是考虑以更具创业精神的方式追求目标，秋分都为你开辟了道路。与权力人物讨论你的成就，或为你思考了数月的雄心勃勃的提案争取支持，你将全力以赴。也要考虑在家中建立新的基础，以支持你的雄心，尤其是9月26日当满月在你的家庭生活宫位与任务严苛的土星相连时。与亲人进行心与心的交流，讨论他们如何帮忙或支持你，以便你有更多空间追求梦想，可能会带来巨大影响。

水瓶座：你可能已经注意到，你正经历一个令人兴奋的变革时期，因为8月的日全食激活了你的合作宫位。现在，秋分将推动你通过一股不安和更强烈的渴望改变，为更多乐趣、学习和满足你的旅行欲望创造空间，因为太阳位于你的冒险宫位。现在是探索新的看世界方式、认识圈子外的人、彻底改变日常生活的时候了，比如旅行或上一次启发性的课程。当太阳在9月28日与你的自我表达宫位中的天王星和谐相处时，你可能会有一个特别令人兴奋的顿悟，如何追随你的心。同时，火星在9月27日后进入你的合作宫位，你将热情高涨地邀请伴侣、好友或同事加入你，共同开辟新路。

双鱼座：无论你想在家庭方面取得进展，还是渴望与伴侣亲密接触，秋分都将为你带来回报！当太阳进入你的共同资金和亲密宫位时，你将获得更大的信心。因此，你可以更好地通过有意义的时刻、深入的对话或温暖的拥抱与特殊的人建立联系，无论是伴侣还是家人。不要犹豫地充分利用这个机会；在8月你的星座中耗竭的日全食之后，这应该特别治愈。由于金星将在10月前穿过你的冒险宫位，你还可以期待为生活注入更多愉悦和舒适。

在2026年的秋分时节，你将与亲近的人共同拓展视野。这或许意味着你们将一起尝试新的烹饪方式，制作美味的早午餐；参加正念课程；或者终于去看那场你一直想去的艺术展览。《读者文摘》为你提供了一个简单易懂的占星学指南，从太阳星座、月亮星座和上升星座的理解，到探索每个星座的优势、挑战和欲望。你将了解在爱情、事业、爱好等方面的理想匹配，以及重大天文事件对你的影响。我们致力于通过具有专业知识和经验的作者，并与相关领域的合格专家合作，生产高质量内容。我们依赖可靠的初级来源，包括实践占星师，以及作者的个人经历。在本篇关于2026年秋分占星的文章中，Maressa Brown利用她作为专业占星师和《星座育儿》一书作者的经验，确保所有信息的准确性和对读者的最佳建议。我们核实所有事实和数据，用可信来源支持，并定期更新以保持准确性。了解更多关于我们团队、贡献者和编辑政策的信息。这篇文章《2026年秋分对你的星座意味着什么》首次出现在《读者文摘》上。

Aries (March 21–April 19)

The fall equinox activates your house of partnership, Aries, which means you’re eager to pair up. Whether you’ve been wanting to launch a business with a close friend, move the ball forward on a professional goal with a colleague or take your romantic bond to the next level, you have the wind in your sails now. Though you tend to excel at flying solo, showing up within your one-on-one relationships can help you make impressive strides on your boldest aspirations, which is music to your ambitious ears.

One word of warning: With the full moon falling in your sign and house of self just a few days after the equinox, your emotions could be running high. Your instinct might be to push through challenging feelings by working out or putting your nose to the grindstone at the office, but allowing yourself to fully acknowledge any heartache that requires healing is your best bet. Reach out to a therapist to work on stress management, or pour what’s in your heart into a beloved imaginative outlet, such as crafting, painting, dancing or journaling.

Taurus (April 20–May 20)

Taurus, you are ruled by Venus, the planet of relationships, which means you’re incredibly devoted to your friends and family. And given how much of a homebody you are, you prefer to host at home whenever possible.

But steel yourself: With the sun moving into fellow Venus-ruled sign Libra and your house of daily routine, the fall equinox can have you running around from one appointment, workout or social commitment to the next. While this could be a little anxiety-inducing, given your typical preference to snuggle up on the couch versus hit the town, your ability to take care of business at a slow, steady, deliberate pace will ensure you’re up to the task.

With Venus in your house of partnership until Oct. 25, you’ll do well to ask for help from a significant other, close friend or trusted colleague to lighten your load. Whether you need an extra set of hands while you prep for a bake sale or company on your morning walk, you’ll feel especially supported now.

Gemini (May 21–June 20)

Prepare yourself for more fun, creativity and playfulness, Gemini, because 2026’s fall equinox astrology is sure to boost your bliss! That’s because the sun will be moving into your house of romance and self-expression—a fun-loving, lighthearted zone that will amplify your artistic impulses and ability to be even more spontaneous and lighthearted than usual (yes, really).

This means you’ll be raring to go when it comes to saying “yes” to booking that last-minute Airbnb stay with friends or an out-of-the-blue romantic weekend getaway with a significant other. Your ruling planet, information-gathering Mercury, will be here too, pulling your mental energy toward this more heart-led way of being in the world. If you can dream it, you can make it happen.

And because the sun is harmonizing with rebellious Uranus in your sign, you’ll feel empowered to march to the beat of your own drum. You might be motivated to try a wardrobe makeover or to dive into an artistic endeavor that has you feeling truly inspired.

Cancer (June 21–July 22)

Although you’re already wired to prioritize quality time with loved ones and feeling cozy in the comfort of your home, the fall equinox will bring even more harmony to your family bonds, Cancer. That’s because the sun lights up your house of home life, making it easier to bond with loved ones, nurture your sense of security and tend to your emotional well-being.

Smoothing over any ongoing conflicts with relatives, infusing your surroundings with more beauty and reveling in beloved fall traditions—like decorating your porch with mums and pumpkins or whipping up your favorite recipes—feel intuitively right. You’ll likely be more centered and happy, because this sentimental, cozy vibe aligns with your innate nature. Feeling more creative and being more spontaneous with loved ones is also in the cards, thanks to Venus being in your house of romance until Oct. 25.

You can also look forward to the fact that Mars is about to start moving through your income house. This will amplify your ability to go to bat for more income-boosting opportunities.

Leo (July 23–Aug. 22)

Being the charismatic friend-magnet that you are, Leo, you’re always eager to make new connections. And with the sun and the moon in your house of communication during the fall equinox, your social life will be especially buzzy.

Not only will it be easier than usual to make a fun game plan with your inner circle, but with your mental energy so high right now, you can also dive into productive brainstorms and come up with brilliant ideas alongside friends and colleagues. The first month of fall could also see you sneaking in a getaway or honing a new skill set like gardening. No matter what you’ve been craving, don’t hesitate to go for it—you’re more likely to get others on board now.

All of this will be happening just ahead of Mars, the planet of action, entering your sign on Sept. 27. This will bring a major surge of get-up-and-go energy that you can channel into your most ambitious goals, whether you want to take your fall wellness routine to the next level or make your mark professionally.

Virgo (Aug. 23–Sept. 22)

Good news, Virgo: The fall equinox will allow you to feel even more self-assured when tackling your moneymaking plans. You’ll be inspired to go after new sources of income and to take stock of your current saving and investing approaches, ensuring they’re in line with your values.

This is also a beneficial moment for reflecting on your self-worth and whether you’re being properly compensated for your time, energy and skills. You may find you can be more assertive when making a play for a raise or promotion, pursuing a side hustle or researching what it would take to start your own business. With both the sun and your ruling planet, Mercury, in this zone, you’ll knock it out of the park.

As industrious as you are, you’ll also want to be sure you’re building in enough downtime, because with Mars in your house of spirituality after Sept. 27, you’ll be nudged to be more intentional with your time and energy. Make a point to prioritize restorative activities like bird watching, a low-impact yoga class or deadzoning.

Libra (Sept. 23–Oct. 22)

Welcome to the limelight, Libra! The fall equinox is tied to the kickoff of your season, and the sun will be cruising through your self-image house, making you the star of the show as well as a magnet for more joyfulness until Oct. 23. From going for that well-deserved recognition on the job to sharing what’s in your heart with loved ones, the sun in your sign has you feeling empowered, confident and unstoppable.

You may even notice that your signature traits—seeking peace and harmony, bringing more balance and beauty into every space you enter and prioritizing partnership—are amplified and applauded now. Make the most of this by asking for the one-on-one time you’re craving from a partner or lending your artistic eye to a creative endeavor, like redecorating your bedroom.

Also of note? It’s a good time to enlist friends or family to support your income-generating goals, perhaps by referring others to your business or pitching in when you’re working toward a deadline, because relationship-oriented Venus is in your house of money until Oct. 25.

Scorpio (Oct. 23–Nov. 21)

Though privacy, intimacy and your inner dream life are aspects of life you value deeply all year long, Scorpio, you’ll be feeling even more reserved than usual around the fall equinox, because the sun is entering your spirituality house.

This sector is all about introspection and psychological well-being, so consider reflecting on how you can better tend to emotional wounds that you’ve been carrying for some time. Though this might sound a bit isolating, with Venus in your sign until Oct. 25, you’re also in a place where you can lean on loved ones to talk your feelings through when you feel comfortable opening up. You’ll also find it’s easier to infuse your life with more pleasure and comfort.

And heads up: Mars will be landing in your career house a few days after the equinox, on Sept. 27, elevating how much energy you’ll have to achieve big-picture goals and earn recognition from higher-ups. You might be empowered to step into a leadership position or entirely redefine what success means for you.

Sagittarius (Nov. 22–Dec. 21)

More jovial, fun-filled quality time with your friends is something you’re always aiming for, Sagittarius, and that’s exactly what the 2026 fall equinox brings you, as the sun moves into your house of friendship while the moon activates your house of communication.

This is your annual opportunity to pour even more of yourself into your platonic bonds, to be a team player, to connect with your community and to network all along the way. Bringing your innate go-big-or-go-home attitude to all these endeavors will also pave the way for you to make strides on long-term wishes—another part of your life that’s activated by the astrology of the fall equinox.

You can also take advantage of Mars, the planet of action and energy, moving into your house of adventure, philosophy and higher education on Sept. 27. For about two months, you can be even bolder than usual when it comes to stepping out of your comfort zone and soaking up knowledge. Consider booking a long-distance trip, working with an inspiring mentor or pursuing a more advanced degree.

Capricorn (Dec. 22–Jan. 19)

You’re a pro at putting your nose to the grindstone, Capricorn, which makes this time of year an especially thrilling one for you, because the sun is traveling through your house of career and your public image. Whether you’ve been itching for higher-ups to acknowledge your efforts on the job or you’re flirting with the idea of taking a more entrepreneurial approach to your goals, the fall equinox opens doors for you. Talk through your achievements with someone in a position of power, or go to bat for that ambitious proposal you’ve been musing about for months, and you’ll come out swinging.

Consider setting new foundations at home that will support your ambitions too, especially around Sept. 26 when the full moon in your house of home life connects with taskmaster Saturn. Having a heart-to-heart with loved ones about how they can help pitch in or otherwise have your back so you have more room to chase your dreams could make a world of difference.

Aquarius (Jan. 20–Feb. 18)

Aquarius, you’ve likely noticed you’re already moving through a season of thrilling change, because August’s solar eclipse activated your house of partnership. Now, the fall equinox will nudge you to shake things up with a surge of restlessness and a skyrocketing desire to make more room for fun, learning and satiating any wanderlust, because the sun is in your house of adventure.

This is the time to explore new ways of seeing the world, meet people outside of your usual friend group and overhaul your typical routine, perhaps by traveling or taking an eye-opening class. When the sun harmonizes with Uranus in your house of self-expression on Sept. 28, you could have an especially exciting epiphany about how to follow your heart.

And with action-oriented Mars in your partnership house after Sept. 27, you’ll be fired up to enlist a significant other, close friend or colleague to join you as you blaze new trails.

Pisces (Feb. 19–March 20)

Whether you want to make strides with family members or you’re craving closeness with your significant other, the fall equinox has rewards in store for you, Pisces! You’ll enjoy greater confidence as the sun enters your house of joint finances and intimacy. In turn, you can better connect with someone special—whether that’s a significant other or family member—through meaningful moments, deep conversation or heartwarming snuggle sessions.

Don’t hesitate to embrace this opportunity fully; it should feel especially therapeutic coming off of August’s draining lunar eclipse in your sign. And with Venus moving through your house of adventure until Oct. 25, you’ll be inspired to broaden your horizons alongside the people you care about the most. That could look like joining forces to experiment in the kitchen and cook up flavorful brunch recipes together, taking a mindfulness class or finally visiting that art exhibit you’ve been wanting to check out.

Why trust us

articles.title: Here’s How Popcorn Became the Ultimate Movie Snack—And Why It Wasn’t Allowed in Theaters Originally
articles.content:
2026 是一部深受欢迎的电影年份，从最新的《蜘蛛侠》到史诗巨作《奥德赛》，再到独特风格的《后院》和《橡树街的尽头》，各类电影应有尽有。但即使是一部糟糕的电影，只要有热腾腾、黄澄澄的爆米花，我也能找到享受的理由。不得不说，我喜欢独享自己的一小包爆米花。

如果你是因为爆米花而选择电影院的，请举手。我会举的。上个周末，我特意在中午去了一家小型的艺术电影院，只为了尝试它的售货处供应。我去看的电影《阿姆齐亚王的对手》没有在我家附近的阿拉莫草坪剧院上映，而阿拉莫草坪剧院的爆米花非常好吃。此外，我当时也不想去购物中心的那家电影院看电影。

是的，爆米花能决定一部电影的体验，但这并非一直如此。实际上，电影院最初并不出售爆米花。听起来不可思议？电影没有爆米花？为了了解这一令人震惊的信息，我咨询了食物历史学家兼《马里兰烹饪之道：多元饮食的声音》一书的作者乔伊斯·M·怀特，以及经典电影历史学家、The Lobby电影教育平台的创始人哈里·马克斯。

请继续阅读，了解爆米花与电影的历史。

爆米花是美国（更准确地说是北美和南美）的产物，其历史可以追溯到数千年前。迄今为止发现的最古老的爆米花，是在秘鲁北部海岸发现的，通过碳14测定法确定其年龄为6700年（约公元前4600年）。在此之前，人类食用爆米花的最早证据来自5600年前的新墨西哥州。

怀特说，用于制作爆米花的玉米品种Zeaevert，是墨西哥和现在的美国西南地区最早驯化的玉米品种之一。“直到19世纪初，它才到达东海岸，当时新英格兰鲸船的船员可能从南美洲将其带到了新英格兰。”

此后，它又经过了100多年的时间才成为电影院的热门零食。让我们回顾一下爆米花成为明星的漫长历程。

爆米花已经是我们文化中不可或缺的一部分，但将其引入电影院则是最近的事。以下是前传。

16世纪，当西班牙探险家到达美洲时，爆米花在阿兹特克人和秘鲁印第安人中如此重要，以至于他们惊叹于当地人使用爆米花的各种方式。西班牙人对这种奇特加工的谷物的早期记录如下：

“在美国报纸中，最早提及爆米花的文章出现在1835年佛蒙特州伯灵顿的一篇关于种子品种的文章中，其中提到‘一位农民种植了一种小型鸡玉米（或像孩子们所说的爆米花，因为烤在铲子上时会爆开得很好看）’。”

如果用铲子烤玉米听起来很麻烦（更何况很脏），早期的美国人也这么认为。在1830年代，人们开始使用带长柄的金属篮子，或者像现在一样用锅煮爆米花。“到了1840和1850年代，爆米花更为广泛地为人所知。”怀特说，“它在街角由‘爆米花男’出售，并在酒店中与葡萄干和坚果一起作为甜点供应。”爆米花很快成为野餐、聚会和节日的必备之物。

“糖衣爆米花、爆米花球，甚至爆米花布丁在当时都很受欢迎。”怀特说，“到了1857年，一家商业企业——新英格兰爆米花公司——开始在‘优雅的锡盒’中出售糖衣爆米花，有趣的是，这种预先爆好的爆米花受到了一些人的反对，因为他们认为这破坏了爆米花的乐趣。”

确实，1857年6月27日，巴吞鲁日《三周报》和《彗星报》发表了一篇批评文章：“成年人和孩子们在冬天漫长的夜晚，围着炉火爆玉米的乐趣被剥夺了。”

到了19世纪末，爆米花已经完全融入了美国家庭的生活和文化中。我记得在劳拉·英格尔斯·怀尔德的《农场男孩》一书中（故事发生在1860年代末），提到了爆米花，但直到1893年芝加哥世界博览会（又称世界哥伦布纪念博览会），爆米花才获得了商业推动。那一年，查尔斯·克雷托斯获得了两年前发明的移动爆米花机的专利。

“1893年对克雷托斯来说是个大年。”马克斯说，“他不仅获得了爆米花机的专利，还在芝加哥世界博览会上首次展示了它，并免费提供样品。”克雷托斯试图吸引人们对他的设备感兴趣，而不是爆米花。“结果，人们尝到了免费的样品，喜欢得不得了，在博览会上排队购买更多爆米花。”

“之后，他开发了马拉的爆米花车，将这种美味零食带到街头。”马克斯说，“但即使在20世纪初，随着电影行业的发展，剧院仍然对出售爆米花，或者说任何零食，没有兴趣。”至少暂时还没有。

随着新世纪的到来，爆米花也随之而来。虽然1896年发明了花生米混合干果（Cracker Jack），但人们也将爆米花作为“真正的”食物来吃。饮食学家、玉米片大亨约翰·哈维·凯洛格的妻子埃拉·伊顿·凯洛格，据说会在碗里用牛奶吃爆米花，就像吃谷物一样。

在克雷托斯的爆米花机流行后，街头小贩可以很容易地跟随着城市人群或在剧院和体育赛事外设摊。马克斯说：“爆米花受到出售者的欢迎，是因为其采购和生产成本低。”“即使在20世纪30年代的大萧条时期，这种美味的小吃也只要5到10美分一包——在经济困难时期，这是一个廉价的奢侈品。”

第二次世界大战进一步巩固了爆米花的流行，因为糖的配给使糖果变得稀缺。电视的出现使爆米花的销量有所下降，但它从未消失。1981年，通用磨坊公司专利了一种可以在不烧焦的情况下爆出玉米的微波爆米花袋，美国最受欢迎的零食变得更加方便在家里食用。

爆米花和电影的结合经历了一段时间。马克斯说：“在20世纪初，去电影院最初是一件特殊的事情。”爆米花这种嘎嘣脆、吵闹且廉价的零食并不在早期剧院经理的计划之中。以下是这种情况如何改变的。

“在我们今天熟悉的连锁电影院兴起之前，电影院——或者说更准确的是电影宫殿——希望向观众展示一种优雅的氛围，类似于歌剧院。”马克斯说，“目的是让电影院有去看现场演出的感觉，因此他们用华丽的地毯和奢华的装饰装点他们的设施。”

这些奢华的装饰非常昂贵，院主们最后想要的就是地板上有黏糊糊的饮料、扶手上有油腻的手指——还有“人们的鞋子将散落的爆米花磨进地板”。此外，零食被认为是“低俗的”，与电影院提供的高雅娱乐不相称。

“还有噪音问题。”马克斯补充道，“早期的电影是无声的，尽管它们通常有现场音乐伴奏，但剧院老板不希望观众在观影时啃嚼和发出包装纸的声音。”

到了1920年代末，电影主要是“有声电影”而非无声电影，马克斯说，对爆米花的反对理由已经不再成立。经济很快成为主导因素。“大萧条使某些形式的娱乐对广大公众变得不可及，因此看电影成为人们能够负担得起的最后一项奢侈品。”

“到1930年——市场崩盘一年后——美国电影院每周有多达9000万观众走进门。”马克斯说，“但他们仍然保持着过去的一丝奢华，因此零食仍然不允许进入剧院。”勤奋的小贩站在外面吆喝爆米花，但马克斯说，剧院会让观众像寄存外套一样寄存零食！

情况在允许一些独立小贩在大堂出售零食后发生了变化。“实际上，是密苏里州堪萨斯城的一位寡妇改变了游戏规则。”马克斯说。朱莉亚·布拉登说服了林伍德剧院的老板，让她在大堂开了一家小店。这家小店很快发展成四家，到了1931年，布拉登的年收入超过14000美元，按今天的标准是33万美元以上。

“虽然技术上来说，没有一个人或剧院被认为将爆米花推向大众，但她可以说是电影院爆米花的‘母亲’。”马克斯说。

最终，院主们意识到零食销售确实能赚钱。他们开始自己爆爆米花，并逐渐淘汰独立小贩。“许多老电影院不得不进行翻新或改造，以容纳爆米花机，因为它们过于注重高级装饰而忽视了适当的通风。”马克斯说。

很多！以下是爆米花有趣的事实和数据。

articles.summary:
It’s been a great year for movies. From the latest Spider-Man to the epic The Odyssey to quirkier offerings like Backrooms and The End of Oak Street, 2026 has had a little something for everyone. But even a terrible movie can be salvaged when the popcorn is hot, buttered and all mine. (What can I say? I like having my small popcorn to myself.)

Raise your hand if you pick your movie theater based on the popcorn. Mine’s up. Just last weekend, I headed to a small art theater in the middle of the morning just so I could sample the offerings at the concession stand. The flick I went to see, Matthew McConaughey’s The Rivals of Amziah King, wasn’t at my local Alamo Drafthouse (which has awesome popcorn, by the way), and I wasn’t in the mood for the popcorn at the mall.

Yes, popcorn can make or break a movie, but it hasn’t always been this way. In fact, popcorn wasn’t even sold at the movies in the early days. Say what? Movies without popcorn? To find out more about this totally shocking information, I consulted Joyce M. White, a food historian and the author of Cooking Maryland’s Way: Voices of a Diverse Cuisine, and Harry Marks, a classic film historian and creator of The Lobby film education platforms on TikTok, Instagram and YouTube.

Read on to learn the history of popcorn and the movies.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, entertainment, cleaning, humor, travel and tech all week long.

When was popcorn invented?

Popcorn is American (more accurately, North and South American), and it goes back thousands of years. The oldest ears of popcorn were found along the northern coast of Peru and have been radio-carbon-dated to 6,700 years ago (or around 4600 BCE). Before that finding, which holds the current official Guinness World Record, the oldest evidence of people eating popcorn was from 5,600 years ago, in New Mexico.

White says the type of corn that makes popcorn, Zea everta, was one of the earliest domesticated types of maize in Mexico and what is now the American Southwest. “It did not reach the Eastern Seaboard until the early 19th century, when New England whalers likely brought it to New England from South America,” White says.

From there, it would be more than 100 years before it became a popular movie snack. Let’s take a look back at popcorn’s long road to stardom.

What is the history of popcorn?

Popcorn has been a part of our culture for hundreds of years, but getting it into movie theaters was a more recent endeavor. Here’s the prequel.

Early history

Popcorn was so important to Aztec and Peruvian Indians that when Spanish explorers arrived in the 16th century, they marveled at all the ways the native populations were using it. Here are contemporary accounts of Spanish reactions to this oddly prepared grain:

  • “They scattered before him parched corn, called momochitl, a kind of corn which bursts when parched and discloses its contents and makes itself look like a very white flower; they said these were hailstones given to the god of water,” according to the Florentine Codex, a history compiled by Franciscan missionary Bernardino de Sahagun.
  • “They toast a certain kind of corn until it bursts. They call it pisancalla, and they use it as a confection,” Bernabé Cobo, a Jesuit missionary, wrote in Historia del Nuevo Mundo.
  • “And also a number of young women danced, having so vowed, a popcorn dance. As thick as tassels of maize were their popcorn garlands. And these they placed upon (the girls’) heads,” de Sahagun wrote again in the Florentine Codex.

East Coast arrival

“One of the earliest mentions of it in an American newspaper is found in an article about seed varieties from Burlington, Vermont, from 1835, where it states that a farmer planted a ‘small kind of chicken corn (or as the children call it, pop-corn, from its bursting so handsomely when roasted on a shovel),'” White says.

If holding a shovel full of corn over a fire sounds tedious (not to mention messy), early Americans thought so too. In the 1830s, people began using a wire basket with a long handle or just popping it in a pan like we do today. “By the 1840s and ’50s, it was much more widely known,” White says. “It was sold on street corners by ‘popcorn men’ and in hotels, where it was served with raisins and nuts for dessert.” Popcorn soon became a staple at picnics, parties and festivals.

“Sugar-coated popcorn, popcorn balls and even popcorn puddings were popular at this time,” White says. “By 1857, a commercial venture, The New England Popcorn Company, sold sugar-coated popcorn in ‘elegant tin boxes,’ which curiously was met with some ambivalence because it claimed that pre-popped popcorn took away the fun of popping it.”

Indeed, the Baton Rouge Tri-Weekly Gazette and Comet published a critique on June 27, 1857: “The pleasure indulged in, by adults as well as minors, over the fire in winter’s tedious nights, of popping corn, is taken away from us.”

Chicago World’s Fair

By the mid- to late 19th century, popcorn was fully integrated into American homes and culture—I remember reading about it in Laura Ingalls Wilder’s Farmer Boy, which took place in the late 1860s—but it didn’t get a commercial boost until the World’s Columbian Exposition, aka the Chicago World’s Fair, in 1893. That’s the year Charles Cretors patented a mobile popping machine he had invented two years earlier.

“1893 was a big year for Cretors,” Marks says. “He not only got the patent for his popcorn machine, but he also debuted it at the Chicago World’s Fair, where he gave away the product for free.” Cretors was trying to entice interest in his device—not the popcorn. “Instead, people got their free sample and loved it so much, they lined up to buy more from Cretors directly while at the Fair,” Marks says.

“From there, he developed horse-drawn popcorn wagons to take the tasty snack on the road,” Marks says. “But even at the turn of the century, as the film industry was growing, theaters had no interest in selling it, or really any snacks for that matter.” At least not yet.

The 20th century

As the new century dawned, popcorn came right along with it. Cracker Jack had been invented in 1896, but people also ate popcorn as “real” food too. Ella Eaton Kellogg, a dietitian and the wife of cereal magnate John Harvey Kellogg, reportedly ate popcorn in a bowl with milk, like cereal.

After Cretors’s popcorn machine took off, street vendors could easily follow crowds around cities or post up outside theaters and sporting events. “Popcorn’s popularity among sellers was due to its low cost to procure and produce,” Marks says. Even when the Depression hit in the 1930s, the delicious treat could be had for 5 or 10 cents a bag—an inexpensive luxury during hard times.

World War II further solidified popcorn’s popularity, as sugar rationing made candy scarce. Sales slumped a bit when television hit the scene, but popcorn never went away. In 1981, General Mills patented a microwave popcorn bag that popped kernels without scorching, and America’s favorite snack got even easier to eat at home.

How did popcorn make its way to movie theaters?

It took some time for popcorn and movies to go together. “Going to the theater was meant to be something special early in the 20th century,” Marks says. Popcorn, the crunchy, loud and cheap treat, didn’t figure into early theater managers’ game plans. Here’s how that changed.

Popcorn was originally “beneath” movie theaters

“Long before the corporate multiplexes we’re familiar with today, movie theaters—or, more accurately, movie palaces—wanted to demonstrate an air of sophistication to audiences, similar to that of an opera house,” Marks says. “The idea was to make the movies feel like going to see a live show, so they decked out their facilities with plush carpeting and extravagant decor.”

All those fancy adornments were expensive, and the last thing owners wanted were sticky drinks on the floor, greasy fingers on the armrests—”and stray popcorn kernels being ground into the floor by people’s shoes,” Marks says. Besides, concessions were thought to be “beneath” the high-brow entertainment movie houses were offering.

“There was also the noise issue,” Marks adds. “Early films were silent, but even though they were often accompanied by live musicians, theater owners didn’t want patrons crunching and crinkling their snacks during the shows.”

But … money talks

By the late 1920s, films were mostly “talkies” instead of silent, so Marks says the fancy, hushed-atmosphere argument against popcorn became moot. Economics soon ruled the day. “The Depression had made certain forms of entertainment unattainable to the wider public, so going to the movies became one of the last affordable luxuries people could bear,” Marks says.

“By 1930—one year after the market crash—American movie theaters were seeing as many as 90 million customers per week walk through their doors,” Marks says. “But they were still holding on to that last vestige of glamour from the past, so snacks were still not allowed into the theaters themselves.” Industrious vendors would stand outside hawking popcorn, but Marks says theaters would make patrons check their snacks like they would their coats!

That changed when some theaters allowed independent vendors to sell in their lobbies. “In fact, it was one Kansas City, Missouri, widow who changed the game for everyone,” Marks says. Julia Braden convinced the owner of the Linwood Theater to let her open a stand in the lobby. That one stand soon turned into four, and by 1931, Braden was earning over $14,000 a year—more than $330,000 today.

“Though technically there isn’t one person or theater credited with introducing popcorn to the masses, she’s kind of the de facto ‘Mother of Movie Theater Popcorn,'” Marks says.

Theaters pull back the welcome mat

Eventually, owners saw that there was real money to be made in concessions. They started popping their own popcorn and pushing out the independent vendors. “Many older theaters had to be renovated or modified to accommodate the poppers, as their focus on upscale decor meant little attention to proper ventilation,” Marks says.

But once that happened, it was game over for independent vendors. “In fact, a theater manager named R.J. McKenna actually leaned into lower ticket prices in the 1930s just to get more people into his theaters so they could buy popcorn and other food items,” Marks says. “McKenna put a popcorn popper in the lobby of his theater, and in 1938, he wound up raking in over $200,000,” Marks says.
Today, concessions are big business. Cinemark, one of the nation’s top theater chains, made about 40% of its revenue last year from concessions, bringing in nearly $1 billion, according to the company’s latest SEC filing. As they say in the biz, that’s a wrap—popcorn-wise.

How much popcorn do people eat these days?

A lot! Here’s a rundown of popcorn fun facts and figures.

  • Americans eat about 14 billion quarts of popped popcorn each year. That’s about three cups (aka one serving) per week for every person in the country.
  • Popcorn makes up 60% of movie theater concessions. The rest goes to candy, drinks and other food.
  • Yellow popcorn for the win. Before the Depression, white corn was more popular. “Theaters actually preferred the yellow corn variety, which was twice as expensive as the white variety, but it popped larger, which filled the containers and bags with less popcorn as a result,” Marks says. That’s still true today.
  • 88% of moviegoers say they order popcorn “regularly.” And 94% say they order concessions more generally, according to Fandango. Clearly, popcorn is the main draw.
  • There’s a National Popcorn Day. And it’s celebrated on Jan. 19.
